strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation gap: resistance to typographic attacks should be assessed alongside preservation of useful text reading. I assess it primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, rather than requiring algorithmic novelty from its standard supervised fine-tuning defense.

Pairing object and text questions on the same underlying scenes is a useful design. The benchmark provides 21,953 training scenes and 3,166 validation scenes, multiple attack difficulty levels, and both multiple-choice and open-ended object evaluation.

Experiments across six LVLM configurations consistently demonstrate the risks of object-only robust training. RIO-RT substantially improves attacked object recognition while generally preserving text-reading performance; for Qwen2.5-VL, attacked MC accuracy increases from 65.9 to 98.5 and attacked Text-VQA accuracy from 78.1 to 85.3.

The supplementary transfer experiments on Typo-D and four additional VQA datasets strengthen the empirical contribution. Construction details, generation prompts, training costs, and parameter-placement ablations provide useful reproducibility information.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity needs stronger verification. Several supplied examples contain visibly mismatched questions and answers: Figures 6, 9, 10, and 11 ask 'what kind of beer is this?' for scenes with answers such as Copenhagen, 22, a time, and a person's name. These might be figure assembly errors rather than dataset errors, but the manuscript provides no human audit or error-rate estimate to resolve this consequential uncertainty.

The experiments do not adequately distinguish contextual selective reading from recognizing and rejecting synthetic overlays. All injected text is a distractor, and training and evaluation share a narrow rendering pipeline. Object and text attacks also use different words and placements, so the attacked conditions do not hold the full image fixed while varying question intent. Evaluations with unseen rendering styles, realistic scene-integrated text, and questions requiring reading an inserted word would better substantiate the claimed capability. Typo-D transfer helps establish object robustness but does not resolve this issue for attacked text reading.

The training comparison lacks controls needed to explain the gains. IT-RT receives only object supervision, whereas RIO-RT adds 8K text-question examples. Comparing against object-attack training mixed with clean TextVQA, and against clean object/text fine-tuning, would distinguish attack-specific selective learning from ordinary multitask training and mitigation of catastrophic forgetting. An adapted question-aware prompting baseline is also missing.

Automatic construction introduces unquantified label and answerability risks. Open Images annotations do not establish that every sampled negative is absent, and the described negative-pool pruning does not explicitly exclude all ancestors of positive labels. Key-text localization can fall back to the largest OCR box, but fallback frequencies and localization accuracy are not reported. Avoiding existing text boxes alone does not establish that an overlay preserves object visibility or leaves the question unambiguous.

The open-ended object metric lacks validation against human judgments. R-CLIP-M rewards retrieval of any one true class and subtracts retrieval of the attack class among five CLIP matches; it can therefore penalize semantic proximity without actual copying and overlook other hallucinated objects. The penalty is especially confounded with the hierarchy-based attack difficulty. Handling of the attack penalty for clean images is also unclear.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the quantitative presentation. Table 1 reports a 570% gain for Llama RIO-RT object-OE attack performance increasing from 13.0 to 53.2, which is approximately 309%. Appendix A.3 describes both shared randomized rendering and a separate fixed white-text rendering policy for text attacks. These issues need correction and reconciliation, although they do not independently invalidate the absolute performance gains.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Language-only LoRA succeeding and selected attention maps changing do not establish that robustness arises specifically from reasoning, nor that vision-based defenses are inherently incompatible with reading. Transfer is also uneven: LLaVA-13B loses 8% average performance on external text-centric benchmarks. The contribution would be stronger with narrower claims and explicit treatment of these exceptions.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation gap: robustness to misleading image text should be assessed alongside preservation of legitimate text reading. Linking object and text questions to the same underlying scenes is a useful contribution to vision-language evaluation.

I assess the work primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks, rather than Algorithms/General, because its main contribution is RIO-Bench. Standard supervised fine-tuning is an appropriate demonstrative baseline; a new optimization algorithm is not necessary for acceptance.

The benchmark has substantial coverage: 21,953 training scenes and 3,166 validation scenes, with multiple question formats and attack difficulties. The supplement documents construction rules, prompts, metrics, and training costs, and appropriately attributes TextVQA and Open Images.

Experiments span six LVLM configurations and show substantial improvements. For Qwen2.5-VL-7B, RIO-RT increases attacked object MC accuracy from 65.9 to 98.5 and attacked text accuracy from 78.1 to 85.3, while approximately preserving clean text accuracy.

The supplementary evaluation goes beyond the proposed benchmark, including Typo-D and four external VQA datasets. These results provide meaningful evidence of transfer, although benefits vary across models.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is insufficiently isolated from simpler explanations. All inserted text is misleading, while legitimate reading targets come from the original image, and object questions use fixed templates. A model could learn to reject the overlay style and distinguish question templates without acquiring the broader contextual capability claimed. There are no tests where similarly rendered added text is relevant, or systematic held-out rendering and question-template evaluations. Typo-D transfer is useful but does not establish selective reading under these conditions.

The training comparison confounds selective robustness with preservation of task coverage. IT-RT receives only object supervision, whereas RIO-RT also receives 8K text-reading examples. Consequently, IT-RT's reading degradation could reflect ordinary task forgetting. Missing controls include object-attack training mixed with clean TextVQA, clean object/text multitask training, and paired versus unpaired scene mixtures. These would establish whether attacked text supervision and the same-scene structure contribute beyond standard multitask fine-tuning.

Dataset validity needs stronger verification. Appendix A.2 excludes deepest ground-truth labels and their descendants from negative sampling but does not explicitly exclude their ancestors, which can also describe objects present in the image. Unannotated objects may likewise become false negatives. Text localization uses heuristic matching and a largest-OCR-box fallback, yet no human audit, fallback frequency, or post-attack answerability assessment is reported. These omissions matter for a benchmark whose central claim is controlled, valid counterfactual evaluation.

The qualitative material contains concrete annotation or presentation inconsistencies. Figures 6 and 9–11 repeat 'what kind of beer is this?' for a billboard, baseball player, watch, and whiteboard, respectively. Figures 7–8 list 'Surfboard' among ground-truth objects for bottle images. These could be figure assembly errors rather than dataset errors, but the manuscript does not establish which; they undermine confidence in the examples used to validate construction.

The object open-ended metric is insufficiently validated. R-CLIP-M rewards retrieving any one ground-truth class among five CLIP-nearest classes and subtracts a corresponding attack-label indicator. It does not directly measure the correctness of the full predicted object list, and semantically related attack labels can incur penalties without being explicitly predicted. No human agreement or alternative metric analysis establishes that this score tracks robustness. Separate marginal task scores also leave the promised within-scene consistency largely unmeasured.

Several conclusions and reported quantities need correction. Language-only versus vision-only LoRA results do not establish that gains arise from reasoning, and selected attention maps are not causal evidence. Table 1 contains incorrect relative gains: Qwen2.5 object-OE attack improvement from 26.0 to 53.9 is approximately 107%, not 129%; Llama's improvement from 13.0 to 53.2 is approximately 309%, not 570%. Appendix A.3 also gives conflicting text-attack rendering specifications. These reporting issues are secondary to the missing controls and benchmark validation, which collectively favor rejection despite the worthwhile evaluation objective.

strengths: The primary contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General: its value lies in the evaluation design and empirical findings, not algorithmic novelty. Jointly evaluating resistance to misleading text and preservation of useful reading addresses a meaningful gap in LVLM robustness evaluation.

The same-scene construction is well motivated. Linking TextVQA questions with Open Images object annotations reduces scene-distribution confounds, while multiple-choice and open-ended questions provide complementary evaluations. The benchmark contains 21,953 training scenes and 3,166 validation scenes with multiple attack conditions.

Experiments across six LVLMs consistently demonstrate the practical benefit of balanced training. For Qwen2.5-VL-7B, RIO-RT raises attacked object MC accuracy from 65.9 to 98.5 and attacked TextVQA accuracy from 78.1 to 85.3, while retaining clean TextVQA performance.

The supplementary generalization experiments materially strengthen the contribution: evaluation on Typo-D and four external VQA datasets extends the evidence beyond the proposed benchmark. Training-size and LoRA-placement ablations, detailed construction procedures, and modest training costs further support practical usefulness.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully establish the claimed acquisition of general context-sensitive reasoning. Synthetic overlays, fixed object-question templates, and task-specific attack generation permit simpler strategies such as rejecting overlay text. Missing controls include object-attack training mixed with clean TextVQA, a question-aware prompting baseline, and evaluation on unseen rendering styles or scene-integrated text attacks. The external reading benchmarks contain only clean inputs, so they do not resolve this issue.

Benchmark quality needs stronger validation. No systematic human audit of answer preservation, negative-option validity, or key-text localization is reported. The negative-sampling description excludes ground-truth labels and descendants but does not explicitly exclude their ancestors. Moreover, Figures 9–11 repeat 'what kind of beer is this?' for unrelated scenes and answers. These may be figure assembly errors, but the authors should establish that the underlying benchmark is unaffected.

R-CLIP-M has an important confound: a correct object description can retrieve a semantically related attack class among its top five CLIP matches and be penalized without actually following the distractor. This particularly complicates the claimed effect of semantic attack difficulty. Reporting correctness and attack-match components separately, validating against human judgments, and specifying the attack label used for clean-image scoring would improve confidence.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Language-only LoRA succeeding and vision-only LoRA underperforming do not establish that reasoning is the causal mechanism or that vision-based defenses are inherently incompatible with reading. Selected relative-attention visualizations are illustrative rather than causal evidence. Generalization is also uneven: LLaVA-1.5-13B loses external reading performance, and its attacked Typo-D score remains below CoT.

Reporting inconsistencies require correction. Appendix A.3 describes both shared randomized rendering and a separate fixed white-text configuration for Text-Attack. Table 1 contains incorrect relative gains: 26.0 to 53.9 is approximately 107%, not 129%. The benchmark and generation code are promised, but the project-page link is missing. These issues do not erase the substantial absolute improvements, but weaken reproducibility and presentation.

strengths: The primary contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than algorithmic novelty: RIO-RT is explicitly a reference baseline. Under this interpretation, jointly evaluating typographic robustness and preservation of scene-text reading is a useful contribution to vision-language evaluation.

The same-scene construction reduces scene-distribution confounds when comparing object recognition and text reading. Combining clean/attacked conditions, multiple-choice/open-ended object questions, controlled difficulty levels, and SceneTAP insertions provides a reasonably comprehensive diagnostic benchmark.

The main empirical finding is supported across six backbones. For example, Table 3 shows that LLaVA-1.5-13B's object-only robust training improves attacked object MC accuracy from 68.0 to 97.8 while reducing clean text accuracy from 54.5 to 15.3. RIO-RT retains comparable object robustness while recovering text performance to 53.2.

Evaluation extends beyond the training attack distribution. SceneTAP results and Appendix Table 7 provide evidence of transfer to Typo-D and preservation of performance on several external text-centric datasets. The additional model-scaling and frontier-model evaluations strengthen the benchmark's relevance.

Construction includes sensible safeguards against text occlusion and a 400-sample, three-annotator human audit with high reported agreement. The appendix supplies substantial construction and training detail, and the paper appropriately acknowledges its restricted threat model.
weaknesses: The experiments establish a performance trade-off more convincingly than its proposed mechanism. IT-RT also changes the training task and output distribution, so its text-performance collapse could reflect task specialization or catastrophic forgetting. A matched clean object-only SFT control and an object-attack plus clean-text mixture would help distinguish these explanations from suppression of text sensitivity and establish the specific value of attacked text training.

R-CLIP-M lacks sufficient validation for a benchmark metric. With top-5 semantic retrieval, a correct object answer can also retrieve a related attack label and incur a penalty without actually mentioning the distractor. This is particularly consequential because attack difficulty explicitly varies semantic proximity. Human correlation, sensitivity to K, and separate reporting of correct-label retrieval and attack-label retrieval are needed. The treatment of multiple ground-truth objects and clean samples is also insufficiently specified.

The counterfactual-control claim is stronger than the construction warrants. Object and text attacks use different distractor content and placement rules; the illustrated clean/attacked MC examples also change option order. Thus, the benchmark matches underlying scenes but does not fully isolate question intent and attack presence. Reporting paired failure transitions or joint success across the four settings would better exploit the matched design than marginal accuracies alone.

Sections 5.4–5.5 overinterpret the mechanistic evidence. Better performance from language-side LoRA does not establish that reasoning primarily governs the behavior, and selected attention visualizations do not demonstrate causal selective filtering. These conclusions should be framed as hypotheses supported by suggestive observations.

Several reporting issues limit reproducibility and confidence in smaller differences. Table 5's Qwen3-VL-8B clean scores differ from Table 3, and some baseline values also differ across Tables 3, 4, and 7 without explanation. The promised detailed human-audit appendix is absent, results lack uncertainty estimates, and the manuscript provides no clear artifact-access or release information. These issues do not overturn the large main effects but should be resolved.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, consistent with its stated focus on benchmarking and analysis. Under that framing, the simple fine-tuning baseline is appropriate; algorithmic novelty is not required. The evidence supports a slight preference for acceptance.

The motivation is meaningful: object-centric attack evaluations can reward defenses that damage useful text reading. Pairing object and text questions on the same underlying scenes provides a useful diagnostic beyond evaluating unrelated datasets separately.

The experimental coverage is substantial: six backbones, multiple attack difficulties, overlay and SceneTAP attacks, additional frontier-model evaluations, and transfer experiments on Typo-D and external VQA datasets.

The central empirical finding is supported by large effects. In Table 3, LLaVA-1.5-13B's text-clean accuracy falls from 54.5 to 15.3 under object-only robust training, whereas mixed training retains 53.2 while substantially improving object-attack robustness.

The construction includes OCR-based protection of existing text and a 400-sample, three-annotator audit. The reported 95.5–97.5% desirable judgments provide useful evidence against widespread invalid examples. Source datasets and reused methods are appropriately attributed.
weaknesses: The proposed R-CLIP-M metric needs stronger validation. Subtracting attack-label top-5 retrieval can penalize a correct prediction merely because the distractor is semantically close to the correct class. This also confounds the interpretation of semantic attack difficulty. Human agreement, exact-label controls, and sensitivity to K are missing. Moreover, Appendix B describes only ground-truth retrieval, omitting the subtraction, and the treatment of multiple ground-truth labels and clean examples is insufficiently specified.

The counterfactual-control claim is stronger than the implementation establishes. Object and text attacks use different distractors and placement policies, so switching intent on attacked examples also changes image content. Figures 6–7 additionally change MC option order between clean and attacked conditions. The benchmark offers matched underlying scenes, but does not fully isolate question intent and attack presence as independent interventions. Fixed-option comparisons and both intents evaluated on identical attacked images would strengthen this claim.

The interpretation of IT-RT degradation as learned text suppression is not isolated from ordinary task-specific forgetting. IT-RT receives only object supervision, whereas RIO-RT adds text supervision. Matched controls using clean object training and object-attack plus clean-text training would clarify whether attacked text examples teach selective robustness beyond preserving text-task competence. Language-only LoRA success and selected attention maps likewise do not establish that reasoning is the governing mechanism.

Reproducibility and numerical consistency need attention. Tables 3, 4, and 7 report differing nominally corresponding results without explaining the protocol changes; Table 5 also differs from Table 3 on Qwen3-VL-8B clean scores. Table 6's evaluation total excludes the listed SceneTAP subsets. The manuscript provides useful construction details but no clear artifact-access or release statement, and the promised detailed audit protocol is absent from the supplied appendix.

The aggregate evaluations underuse the benchmark's paired design. Joint per-scene success and clean-to-attacked transition rates would more directly measure whether the same model handles both requirements reliably. Generalization is encouraging but uneven: Appendix Table 7 shows declines for some backbones on clean external tasks, so broad preservation claims should remain qualified.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: the manuscript explicitly identifies benchmarking and analysis as its main focus. Its value lies in the evaluation design and findings, so the simplicity of the fine-tuning baseline is not a substantive weakness.

The central motivation is compelling: object-centric robustness evaluations can reward defenses that impair useful text reading. RIO-Bench addresses this blind spot through matched scenes with object/text questions and clean/attacked conditions, providing a useful contribution to multimodal robustness evaluation.

The construction includes meaningful quality safeguards: preserving OCR regions, filtering hierarchical negative labels, evaluating both overlays and SceneTAP insertions, and auditing 400 examples with three independent annotators. The reported 95.5–97.5% desirable judgments and high inter-annotator agreement support benchmark validity.

The empirical evidence is broad and supports the principal finding. Across six backbones, object-only robust training frequently damages Text-VQA performance, while balanced training substantially mitigates this loss. For Qwen3-VL-8B, for example, RIO-RT achieves 98.8% attacked object MC accuracy while retaining 84.1% clean text accuracy; IT-RT reduces clean text accuracy to 68.5%.

Evaluation on unseen SceneTAP insertions, external benchmarks, and additional model scales strengthens the contribution beyond a single training distribution. The paper appropriately presents RIO-RT as a reference baseline and acknowledges limits to its threat model and downstream scope.
weaknesses: The experiments do not fully distinguish selective text handling from ordinary task retention during fine-tuning. IT-RT receives only object supervision, whereas RIO-RT receives text-question supervision as well. A budget-matched baseline combining attacked object questions with clean TextVQA would clarify whether attacked text examples are necessary, rather than simply retaining text-task exposure. This limits the explanation of the gains more than the benchmark's usefulness.

R-CLIP-M needs stronger validation. With top-5 semantic retrieval, a correct object answer can also retrieve a related attack label and therefore incur a penalty without actually mentioning the distractor. Because object attack difficulty is itself defined through semantic proximity, some measured difficulty effects may reflect the metric. Human agreement, separate correctness and distractor-inclusion scores, and sensitivity to K would strengthen the OE findings; MC results provide useful independent support.

The claims about language-model reasoning are stronger than the evidence. Language-side LoRA outperforming vision-only LoRA establishes an effective adaptation location under the chosen training recipe, but does not establish reasoning as the underlying mechanism. A few normalized attention visualizations likewise cannot demonstrate causal selective filtering. These conclusions should be phrased as hypotheses.

The counterfactual control is useful but not exact. Appendix examples change MC option order between clean and attacked conditions, and object/text attacks use different inserted content. SceneTAP may also modify non-text evidence within its edit mask. Holding option order fixed and reporting per-scene joint success or clean-to-attack transitions would better exploit the matched design and support the isolation claims.

Reproducibility and reporting need clarification. The supplied manuscript lacks a concrete dataset/code access statement and detailed audit instructions despite referring readers to the appendix. Table 6's evaluation total of 34,826 appears to omit the three SceneTAP rows: all listed rows sum to 44,324. Some repeated results also differ across tables without explanation, including Qwen3-VL-8B clean scores in Tables 3 and 5. These are correctable issues, but important for a benchmark intended as a standardized testbed.
